claim: Plasmodium vivax is the predominant species causing malaria in the Americas and Asia-Pacific regions.
source: Plasmodium vivax is the predominant species causing malaria in the Americas and Asia-Pacific regions (WHO, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO 2014 report

claim: P. vivax is less susceptible to commonly-used vector control measures due to its unique biology.
source: Due to its unique biology, P. vivax is less susceptible to commonly-used vector control measures (Mueller et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mueller et al., 2009

claim: The development and deployment of an effective vaccine against P. vivax has become a high priority.
source: With renewed funding and commitment towards the goal of eliminating malaria, the development and deployment of an effective vaccine against P. vivax has become a high priority (malERA Consultative Group on Vaccines, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to malERA Consultative Group on Vaccines, 2011

claim: Clinical immunity to P. vivax is acquired more rapidly than to P. falciparum.
source: Clinical immunity to P. vivax is acquired more rapidly than to P. falciparum and, in moderate and highly endemic areas, clinical disease is virtually absent in children older than five years (Phimpraphi et al., 2008; Lin et al., 2010; Robinson et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Phimpraphi et al., 2008; Lin et al., 2010; Robinson et al., 2015

claim: In moderate and highly endemic areas, clinical disease is virtually absent in children older than five years.
source: Clinical immunity to P. vivax is acquired more rapidly than to P. falciparum and, in moderate and highly endemic areas, clinical disease is virtually absent in children older than five years (Phimpraphi et al., 2008; Lin et al., 2010; Robinson et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Phimpraphi et al., 2008; Lin et al., 2010; Robinson et al., 2015

claim: Sub-microscopic infections are common even in areas where malaria transmission has been substantially reduced.
source: Sub-microscopic infections are common even in areas where malaria transmission has been substantially reduced (Cheng et al., 2015; Bousema et al., 2014), suggesting the development of effective immunity that provides good control of parasitemia.
evidence: Supported by citations to Cheng et al., 2015; Bousema et al., 2014

claim: The humoral component is thought to be essential for the development of anti-P. vivax immunity.
source: Whilst our understanding of the protective immune effector mechanisms is incomplete, the humoral component is thought to be essential for the development of anti-P. vivax immunity, and antibodies confer protection by both preventing high-density parasitemia and inhibiting blood-stage replication (Longley et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Longley et al., 2016

claim: Antibodies confer protection by both preventing high-density parasitemia and inhibiting blood-stage replication.
source: Whilst our understanding of the protective immune effector mechanisms is incomplete, the humoral component is thought to be essential for the development of anti-P. vivax immunity, and antibodies confer protection by both preventing high-density parasitemia and inhibiting blood-stage replication (Longley et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Longley et al., 2016

claim: Evidence of relatively long-lived IgG levels and/or seropositivity to P. vivax proteins have been reported even in the absence of detectable P. vivax infections.
source: Evidence of relatively long-lived IgG levels and/or seropositivity to P. vivax proteins such as circumsporozoite protein (CSP), merozoite surface protein 1 (MSP1), apical membrane antigen 1 (AMA1) and Duffy binding protein (DBP) have been reported even in the absence of detectable P. vivax infections (Longley et al., 2015; Wipasa et al., 2010; Achtman et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Longley et al., 2015; Wipasa et al., 2010; Achtman et al., 2005

claim: A highly-efficacious malaria vaccine has unfortunately not yet been achieved for any of the Plasmodium spp. parasites.
source: A highly-efficacious malaria vaccine has unfortunately not yet been achieved for any of the Plasmodium spp. parasites, and the vast majority of vaccines in development are based on single recombinant protein antigens (Halbroth and Draper, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Halbroth and Draper, 2015

claim: The vast majority of vaccines in development are based on single recombinant protein antigens.

claim: For P. falciparum, more than 15 antigens are under pre-clinical or clinical testing.
source: For P. falciparum, more than 15 antigens are under pre-clinical or clinical testing, including the pre-erythrocytic, CSP-based RTS,S/AS01 vaccine, which has recently completed Phase 3 trials (Agnandji et al., 2012; RTS,S Clinical Trials Partnership, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Agnandji et al., 2012; RTS,S Clinical Trials Partnership, 2014

claim: The pre-erythrocytic, CSP-based RTS,S/AS01 vaccine has recently completed Phase 3 trials.

claim: The potential of novel, pre-erythrocytic candidate antigens, including P. vivax cell-traversal protein for ookinetes (CelTOS) and thrombospondin-related anonymous protein (TRAP) is being investigated in animal models.
source: The potential of novel, pre-erythrocytic candidate antigens, including P. vivax cell-traversal protein for ookinetes (CelTOS) and thrombospondin-related anonymous protein (TRAP) is being investigated in animal models (Mueller et al., 2015; Alves et al., 2017; Bauza et al., 2014).

claim: Recent serological screens of large panels of P. falciparum proteins in naturally-exposed populations have identified several antigenic targets associated with protective immunity.
source: Recent serological screens of large panels of P. falciparum proteins in naturally-exposed populations have identified several antigenic targets associated with protective immunity, and strongly support the hypothesis that a multicomponent vaccine possibly including antigens from different stages of the parasites life cycle would offer a higher degree of protection than a single component vaccine (Halbroth and Draper, 2015; Richards et al., 2013; Osier et al., 2014a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Halbroth and Draper, 2015; Richards et al., 2013; Osier et al., 2014a

claim: A multicomponent vaccine possibly including antigens from different stages of the parasites life cycle would offer a higher degree of protection than a single component vaccine.

evidence: Supported by citations to Halbroth and Draper, 2015; Richards et al., 2013; Osier et al., 2014a

claim: The availability of the genome sequence and transcriptome have enhanced our understanding of the parasite's biology.

claim: The study of targets of human natural immunity in exposed populations must play an essential role in identifying and prioritizing P. vivax antigens for further functional characterization for vaccine or biomarker development.
source: Given the lack of methods to continuously culture P. vivax to study specific proteins in vitro, or animal models for extensive in vivo assays, the study of targets of human natural immunity in exposed populations must play an essential role in identifying and prioritizing P. vivax antigens for further functional characterization for vaccine or biomarker development (Chia et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chia et al., 2014

claim: Antibodies to proteins such as MSP3α, MSP9 (30) and DBP have shown strong associations with reduced risk of clinical disease or blood-stage infection.
source: Antibodies to proteins such as MSP3α, MSP9 (30) and DBP (King et al., 2008; Cole-Tobian et al., 2009) have shown strong associations with reduced risk of clinical disease or blood-stage infection.
evidence: Supported by citations to King et al., 2008; Cole-Tobian et al., 2009

claim: Screening studies to extend the pool of P. vivax vaccine candidates remain scarce.

claim: The study investigated the association between IgG to 38 P. vivax recombinant antigens and risk of vivax malaria in a cohort of young Papua New Guinean children.
source: To explore the reservoir of antigenic targets and prioritize candidates for functional characterization, we investigated the association between IgG to a comprehensive library of 38 P. vivax recombinant antigens and risk of vivax malaria in a cohort of young Papua New Guinean (PNG) children with well-characterized differences in exposure to P. vivax infections (Lin et al., 2010).
evidence: Describes the study design and methods used

claim: The potential existence of synergistic or additive effects of combinations of antibody responses to a large panel of P. vivax antigens has never been explored.
source: To our knowledge, the potential existence of synergistic or additive effects of combinations of antibody responses to a large panel of P. vivax antigens has never been explored.

claim: Except for MSP3α, all other antigens in the top-10 were either novel or understudied proteins, including EBP, PVX_081550, PVX_122805, CyRPA, RBP1a, RBP2b and P41.

claim: The protection observed for P. vivax is species-specific.

claim: A panel of 38 recombinant P. vivax antigens was included in this study.
source: A panel of 38 recombinant P. vivax antigens was included in this study.
evidence: Description of study materials

claim: Both leading vaccine candidate proteins and proteins that are known or predicted to be involved in erythrocyte invasion were included.
source: Both leading vaccine candidate proteins (i.e. five allelic variants of DBPII, CSP, AMA1 and MSP1), and proteins that are known or predicted to be involved in erythrocyte invasion were included (five different constructs of MSP3α, MSP9, ARP, GAMA, P12, P41, CyRPA, RBP1a, RBP2a, RBP2b, RBP2cNB [i.e. not containing the binding domain], RBP2-P2, and EBP; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Description of antigen selection criteria

claim: Bioinformatics approaches were used to identify novel proteins on the basis of expression profile, signal peptide, putative GPI anchor, and homology to known P. falciparum antigens.
source: Additionally, bioinformatics approaches were used to identify novel proteins on the basis of expression profile, signal peptide, putative GPI anchor, and homology to known P. falciparum antigens (which were thus likely to be exposed to the immune-system during erythrocyte invasion or in schizonts (Hostetler et al., 2015; Arumugam et al., 2014) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Description of antigen selection methods with citations to Hostetler et al., 2015; Arumugam et al., 2014

claim: Antigens were produced in different collaborating laboratories using mostly HEK 293E cells, E. coli, or a WGCF expression system.
source: Antigens were produced in different collaborating laboratories using mostly HEK 293E cells, E. coli, or a WGCF expression system as previously described (Hostetler et al., 2015; Gruszczyk et al., 2016; Arumugam et al., 2014).
evidence: Description of antigen production methods with citations

claim: Protein folding has been validated by demonstrating that plasma from naturally-exposed populations recognize the native protein.
source: Protein folding has been validated previously by demonstrating that plasma from naturally-exposed populations recognize the native protein, and antibodies to some of them are strongly associated with reduced risk of vivax malaria (Lu et al., 2014; Stanisic et al., 2013; Cole-Tobian et al., 2009; Hostetler et al., 2015; França et al., 2016a; Yadava et al., 2007); by demonstrating that vaccine-induced antibodies raised against the recombinant protein recognize the native protein (Bennett et al., 2016); by showing that the proteins have appropriate biological function through the identification of protein-protein interactions (Hostetler et al., 2015); or by obtaining a crystal structure (Gruszczyk et al., 2016).
evidence: Description of validation methods with multiple citations

claim: The number of combinations from a panel of 38 antigens is enormous (238 ~ 2.7 × 1011), making investigation of every combination computationally infeasible.
source: The number of combinations from a panel of 38 antigens is enormous (238 ~ 2.7 × 1011), making investigation of every combination computationally infeasible.
evidence: Mathematical calculation of combinatorial space

claim: It is possible to investigate all possible combinations of antigens of size up to five, where there are approximately 500,000 combinations.
source: In practice, it is possible to investigate all possible combinations of antigens of size up to five, where there are approximately 500,000 combinations (Osier et al., 2014a).
evidence: Statement about computational feasibility with citation to Osier et al., 2014a

claim: A simulated annealing algorithm was used to explore the combination space of 38 antigens to identify combinations with optimal potential protective efficacy.
source: A simulated annealing algorithm (Kirkpatrick et al., 1983) was used to explore the combination space of 38 antigens to identify combinations with optimal potential protective efficacy, defined as the proportional reduction in cases of P. vivax clinical malaria comparing children with high versus low antibody levels.
evidence: Description of computational method with citation to Kirkpatrick et al., 1983
